description: We are a collaborative and adaptable team with backgrounds and interests in data analysis, software development, and spatial research. Participating in the Be an Earth System Trend Detective challenge, we focus on open science, continuous learning, and effective teamwork. We value turning technical processing into clear, cross-disciplinary, and practical outcomes.
summary:
VULPA is a free web app that tests whether a change in Earth’s climate is real. It shows NASA data on an interactive 3D globe for 104 ecological regions and any coordinate on Earth. Seiron, its voice-controlled AI assistant (English/Turkish), flies the globe, opens data layers and explains results in plain words.

The challenge asks us to detect and explain trends in Earth system data. VULPA does this with real NASA observations: NASA POWER/MERRA-2, GPM IMERG, GRACE/GRACE-FO, AIRS, MODIS, OMI, GLDAS and EONET. Every series is checked by three methods: a seasonal Mann-Kendall test, a Sen slope with a 95% confidence interval and an autocorrelation-corrected t-test. A trend is called significant only when the methods agree, and a data-confidence badge shows how reliable the result is. Users can compare any two years and see a 10-year trend extension, clearly labelled as not a forecast.

Climate claims spread faster than evidence. NASA’s raw satellite files are hard for most people to use. VULPA turns them into tested, understandable answers for students, teachers, journalists and local planners. It is free, needs no code or downloads, and works on any phone.
details:
VULPA (Earth System Trend Detective) is a web app that answers one question: is a change in Earth’s climate real, or just noise? The user picks one of 104 ecological regions on an interactive 3D globe, or types any coordinate on Earth, and chooses a variable: temperature, precipitation, groundwater, vegetation, atmospheric temperature at different heights, ozone, NO₂ and more. VULPA loads the monthly NASA time series for that place and runs a statistical test chain. The result appears as a clear verdict (increasing, decreasing or no significant trend), the rate of change per decade, a 95% confidence interval and a data-confidence badge.

Our scientific method has three independent parts. First, the seasonal Mann-Kendall test (Hirsch, Slack & Smith, 1982) detects a monotonic trend while handling the seasonal cycle separately. Second, the Sen slope (Sen, 1968) gives an outlier-resistant rate of change, with a 95% confidence interval following Gilbert (1987). Third, a linear-regression t-test with an autocorrelation-corrected effective sample size (Santer et al., 2000) checks the result independently. A trend is called significant only when the methods agree. When they disagree, VULPA says so instead of hiding it. Following Weatherhead et al. (1998), it also estimates how many years of data are needed before a trend of that size can be detected. Users can compare any two years on a difference map, see a 10-year trend extension with an uncertainty fan (clearly labelled as not a forecast), and cross-check results with NASA Giovanni.

The data come from NASA POWER/MERRA-2, GPM IMERG, GRACE/GRACE-FO, AIRS, MODIS, OMI, GLDAS and EONET natural events. NOAA, NSIDC, PSMSL, Copernicus ERA5, Open-Meteo and Meteomatics complement them for live weather, sea level, sea ice and CO₂. Live layers show the temperature anomaly as a thermal surface and pressure systems with isobars on the globe. Seiron, our bilingual (English/Turkish) voice-controlled AI assistant, flies the globe, opens layers and explains concepts such as the p-value in plain words. Its answers are grounded in VULPA’s own NASA numbers. A “detective mode” guides students step by step to a question worth investigating.

The main benefits are trust and accessibility. NASA’s raw satellite files require programming skills, but VULPA turns them into tested answers anyone can understand. It is free, needs no code, no downloads and no sign-up, and works on any phone through a QR-linked mobile view. Every source is cited with its licence in the Credits panel.

The intended impact is to fight climate misinformation by putting evidence in people’s hands. Climate claims spread faster than evidence. VULPA lets students, teachers, journalists and local planners check a claim about their own place in seconds, which supports UN SDG 13 (Climate Action) and SDG 4 (Quality Education).

We built VULPA in Python with Streamlit, Plotly (3D orthographic globe and charts), pandas, NumPy, SciPy and pyMannKendall, plus custom HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the globe controller and interface. Seiron uses large language models through the Groq API (gpt-oss-120b with fallback models) and a local rule-based engine as a final fallback. The app is hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud, and the code is managed with Git and GitHub. We used Claude and Claude Code (Anthropic) for coding, translation and design assistance. No special hardware was needed; everything was developed on standard laptops.

VULPA is creative because it combines things usually found in separate tools: a live 3D globe, rigorous statistics, plain-language AI explanations and voice control. It also treats honesty as a feature: it shows when methods disagree, when data are thin, and when a line is only a trend extension.
